deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text, formulas or labels. It holds only pencil sketches.

Upper left is a cluster of four freehand circles: three stacked vertically, overlapping or tangent, and a fourth to the lower left of the stack. Each circle is crossed by curved arcs. In the stacked circles these look like meridians running from a top point to a bottom point (lunes, or digons, between pseudo-great-circles). In the left circle the arcs form a star-like pattern of several crossing curves, suggesting a few pseudo-great-circles cutting out triangles.

Lower left is a separate circle with two meridian-like arcs meeting at its poles. These two arcs bound a pair of antipodal digons.

The rest of the page shows only show-through from the reverse or adjacent sheet. These faint marks include dashed 'U' and hourglass shapes, dashed crossing segments and arrows. They resemble the dotted transition-arc and triangle diagrams of pages 104 and 106.

In context (cote 154, systems of pseudo-lines; p.104 discusses antipodal transition arcs on Pol(D') and cycles of positions (D,a,w)), these are most plausibly sketches of the sphere, the double cover of the projective plane, carrying pseudo-great-circles. A pseudo-line in P^2 lifts to a centrally symmetric simple closed curve on S^2. Two such curves meet in exactly two antipodal points, giving four lunes, as in the lower sketch. Three in general position cut the sphere into eight triangles, as the star-shaped left sketch may attempt to show. The vertical chain of spheres might depict successive positions in a cycle of configurations, like the (1)→(2)→(3)→(4)→(1) cycle on p.104, or simply repeated attempts at drawing the picture.

No statement, construction or computation is recorded, so there is nothing to verify.
